source: Resolve each force into components; the x and y directions each obey Newton's second law separately.
Students forget that a rope pulling up at an angle also lowers the normal force.
Ropes pull at angles, handles push at angles. A force at an angle acts partly along each axis, so you split it with components and use the second law along each axis separately.
Resolve every force into $x$- and $y$-components. Then $\Sigma F_x = ma_x$ and $\Sigma F_y = ma_y$ are two separate equations. A force at an angle changes both sums, including the normal force.

The $x$ and $y$ directions are independent, as they were for adding vectors: the horizontal part of a pull can only change horizontal motion, and its vertical part only vertical motion. A rope pulling up at an angle lifts part of the object's weight, so the floor pushes up less, and friction ($\mu N$) gets smaller too.
A 20 kg box pulled with 50 N at 30°: the rope lifts 25 N, so the normal force is 196 − 25 = 171 N.
A rope pulls a $20\ \text{kg}$ box along a level floor with $50\ \text{N}$ at $30^\circ$ above the horizontal. Find the normal force.

You push a $15\ \text{kg}$ mower with $60\ \text{N}$ along its handle, $35^\circ$ below the horizontal. Find the normal force.

Forgetting that a rope pulling up at an angle also lowers the normal force (and that a push down at an angle raises it), then using $\mu mg$ for friction. Check: write the $y$-equation before the $x$-equation, and find $F_N$ from it first.
